title: Patient repositioning

sources.use: International Guideline 4th ed. Quick Reference Guide (recommendations and good-practice statements), re-fetched and read in full text 2026-11-16

objectives: Protect lines, tubes and skin while turning.

items.text: Use friction- and shear-reducing equipment and suitable lifting methods when moving the patient.
Check under and around devices and securements after each move.
Reposition on an individualised schedule based on mobility, skin and tissue tolerance, clinical condition, comfort, sleep, goals of care and the support surface.

The guideline notes that critically ill individuals, or others with systemic hypoperfusion or shock states, may need more frequent, incremental repositioning, and may benefit from supplementing full-body repositioning with assisted small shifts in body position; it also calls for assessing for early signs of skin and tissue injury, which may mean a patient needs more frequent repositioning or preferential positioning off a damaged area.
Turning technique, staff numbers, lateral and prone positioning and line management follow the unit's approved procedure and manual-handling policy.
Observe skin, haemodynamics and ventilation during and after repositioning; after every move check tube depth and securement.
Stop and call for help if the patient becomes unstable, a line or tube moves, or skin damage is found.
Record position, time, skin findings and tolerance per your unit's documentation standard.

checklist.text: Plan the turn, count lines and tubes and agree roles with the team per unit procedure.
Use friction- and shear-reducing equipment per policy.
Check tube depth, securement and device positions after the move.
Inspect skin under and around devices.
Stop and call for help if the patient becomes unstable.
Record the position, time and findings.

gaps: Prone positioning procedure: not covered by the sources read.
